newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Trade data, sentiment index.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Trade data, sentiment index.

text.p: U.S. credit markets are expected to shrug off Friday's economic data on international trade and consumer sentiment and focus on the September T-bond contract level, analysts said.
"There is nothing much in the way of (economic) data so it will probably be strict technicals," said John Park, an economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.
With the September bond contract near 115, aggressive trading could persist as traders with opposing positions try to get the market to move in their direction, analysts said.
"Right now (traders) are trying to beat it down below (115)," said Park. "Whoever is trying to keep it down is doing a pretty good job."

On the data front, the Commerce Department publishes its international trade balance for May at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. Experts surveyed by Reuters are calling for a modest uptick in the trade gap to $9.18 billion from $8.36 billion in April.

"The trade numbers will give you a little more definite answer as to what happened to (gross domestic product) growth in the first quarter," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenerette Securities.

Unless the shortfall comes in more than a billion dollars away from the consensus, analysts said the market should easily digest the results. Otherwise, economists might have to adjust their GDP projections.
"When the April trade deficit came out it forced a lot of people to revise GDP higher," said Matthew Alexy, chief markets stategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
"So if you saw a widening of the gap beyond expectations, that would force another revision to GDP," he said.
The Labor Department is slated to release Import/Export prices for June, at 1000 EDT. May import prices were unchanged, and export prices fell 0.2 percent.
Also at 1000 EDT, comes the preliminary snapshot on consumer sentiment in July from the University of Michigan. A reading of 104.6 is expected, slightly higher from the 104.5 reading in June.
While recent reports suggest consumers are beaming with confidence, the reality is that they have been reluctant to spend, reducing the credibility of such confidence measures, some experts said.
"Michigan is up towards the high end and it hasn't been this high in a long time," said Alexy.
The confidence numbers are "losing credibility," Alexy said, adding that "confidence keeps going up, but nothing is going on in the economy."
